en.a: It depends almost entirely on the quality of care. Historically, stressed circus, logging, or poorly managed zoo elephants died far younger than wild ones. But modern accredited zoos report a median life expectancy of about 47 years for female Asian elephants, per the Smithsonian's National Zoo, and the verified captive record is 86. A well-run captive home can approach wild lifespan; a poor one is dramatically shorter.

en.q: What is the oldest elephant ever recorded?
en.a: The oldest elephant ever verified was Lin Wang, an Asian bull who died at Taipei Zoo in Taiwan on February 26, 2003, at the age of 86, according to Guinness World Records. According to Guinness, he carried supplies for the Japanese army through the jungles of Myanmar (Burma) during World War II, was later taken by Chinese forces in 1943, and retired to Taipei Zoo in 1954. African elephants in captivity have reached a recorded maximum of about 65 years, with unpublished reports of individuals approaching 80 years (Animal Diversity Web).

en.q: What usually kills old elephants?
en.a: In old age, elephants most often die of starvation caused by tooth wear. Elephants get six sets of molars in a lifetime, pushed forward like a conveyor belt as each set wears down; once the sixth and final set is exhausted, the animal can no longer chew tough vegetation and starves. In the wild, males also die at higher rates from fighting injuries and the metabolic strain of musth, their periodic state of heightened aggression and reproduction.

en.q: How long do common house spiders live?
en.a: Most common house spiders (Parasteatoda tepidariorum) live about one year or more after reaching maturity, according to Penn State Extension. Similar indoor cobweb weavers and cellar spiders typically persist 1-3 years, with barn funnel weavers occasionally reaching seven years in sheltered conditions.

en.q: What species of spider lives the longest?
en.a: Female tarantulas are the longest-lived spiders. The Mexican red-knee tarantula (Brachypelma smithi) reaches 25-30 years in females while males rarely exceed about 10, per the Animal Diversity Web. Trapdoor spiders are also exceptionally long-lived — commonly cited at up to about twenty years, with one Australian trapdoor spider documented at 43 — thanks to secure, climate-buffered burrows.

en.q: Do male or female spiders live longer?
en.a: Females almost always outlive males. In tarantulas, females live decades longer (25-30 years versus ~10 for males); in widows and jumping spiders, males typically die soon after their final molt and mating, while females guard egg sacs and may overwinter. This gap is thought to stem largely from the energy males expend roaming to find mates, while females remain relatively sedentary and invest in egg production and guarding.

en.q: How can I help a pet spider live longer?
en.a: Provide a stable species-appropriate temperature, correct humidity, a secure hiding burrow or web corner, clean water, and regular small prey, while minimising handling and falls. Captive spiders routinely exceed wild lifespans because they're protected from predators, parasitic worms, frost, and starvation — a widow that lives about a year outdoors can reach four or more years in a terrarium.

en.q: How long does a mosquito live indoors?
en.a: An adult female that gets inside can live about 2 to 4 weeks, the same as outdoors, if she can find a blood meal and a little standing water for her eggs. Stable room temperature and humidity actually suit her. Males, which don't bite, are generally shorter-lived (in the common malaria mosquito, Anopheles quadrimaculatus, males average about 7 days). (CDC; Animal Diversity Web)

en.q: How long can a mosquito live without food or blood?
en.a: Adults of both sexes get most of their energy from plant nectar and sugars, not blood. Deprived of any food or water, an adult typically dies within a few days. Females need a blood meal only to develop their eggs, not to stay alive day to day. (CDC; Penn State Extension)

en.q: How long can mosquito eggs survive before hatching?
en.a: Longer than you'd expect. Aedes mosquito eggs, glued to container walls just above the waterline, can survive drying out for up to 8 months and even endure a southern U.S. winter, the CDC notes, hatching when water rises over them again. Anopheles eggs, by contrast, do not tolerate drying out and hatch within days. (CDC; Penn State Extension)

en.q: Do male or female mosquitoes live longer?
en.a: Females live noticeably longer. The CDC notes females "often live longer than males," and in the common malaria mosquito (Anopheles quadrimaculatus) females average about 21 days versus roughly 7 for males, per Animal Diversity Web. Only females bite; males feed on nectar, mate, then die quickly.

en.q: How long does a worker honey bee live?
en.a: A worker honey bee lives about six weeks during the active summer foraging season, on average about 15 to 38 days. Workers spend their first two to three weeks on inside-hive duties (nursing larvae, building comb, guarding) and then forage until worn out. Workers born in fall are different: they store extra fat and can live four to six months (150 to 200 days) through winter to rear the first spring brood.

en.q: How long does a queen bee live?
en.a: A queen honey bee typically lives two to three years, and some reach up to five years; one study recorded a maximum of eight. Her productive egg-laying usually drops after about two years, which is why most beekeepers re-queen a colony every one to two years. The queen's long life comes from her royal-jelly diet, which sets up high levels of protective proteins (including vitellogenin) and strong resistance to oxidative stress.

en.q: How long do drone bees live, and do they die after mating?
en.a: Drone bees (the males) live roughly three to four and a half weeks, on average about 21 to 32 days during the spring and summer when they are produced. They become sexually mature about a week after emerging, then fly to drone congregation areas to mate. A drone that successfully mates with a queen dies immediately afterward. Any drones that do not mate are expelled from the hive before winter, so very few males survive the cold months.

en.q: Do bees live longer in the winter?
en.a: Winter worker bees live far longer than summer workers — about four to six months (150 to 200 days) compared with roughly six weeks. Born in late summer and fall, these so-called fat bees store extra proteins and fat and stay inside the warm winter cluster rather than foraging, which avoids the wear and predation that kill summer bees. They survive to raise the colony's first spring bees, then die.

en.q: How long does resin take to cure before I can demold it?
en.a: Most coating and tabletop epoxies are hard enough to demold at about 24 hours, when the piece reaches roughly 95% solidity and is hard to the touch. However, 24 hours is a demold/handle stage, not full cure; wait the full 72 hours before sanding, drilling, or putting the piece under load. Fast hardeners may allow demold sooner, slow systems later.

en.q: Why is my resin still tacky after 24 hours?
en.a: A sticky surface almost always comes from one of four causes: off-ratio measuring (TotalBoat requires a strict 2:1 resin-to-hardener ratio by volume), incomplete mixing, cold shop temperatures below the hardener's minimum (55 degF for TotalBoat, 60 degF for West System 206), or a pour that is too thin to generate enough exothermic heat. Fix the cause and recoat or pour a fresh layer over the tacky surface.

en.q: How can I make resin cure faster?
en.a: Warm the resin and workspace slightly (a warm water bath before mixing helps), switch to a fast hardener, and keep pours within the recommended depth so heat can dissipate. ArtResin notes that warmth reduces working time by about 10-15 minutes (and speeds the overall cure, though it does not quantify that reduction). A fast hardener like TotalBoat's reaches tack-free in about 2 hours and full cure in roughly 2 days at 77 degF.

en.q: Can I pour a second coat of resin before the first fully cures?
en.a: Yes, and it is usually preferred. Apply the second coat while the first is still slightly tacky (typically within the first 24 hours) so the two layers chemically bond with no sanding. If the first coat has passed full cure (around 72 hours), sand it lightly and wipe with solvent first to give the new layer mechanical grip before pouring.

en.q: Can you use cold process soap before 4 weeks?
en.a: Technically yes, but it is not recommended. Saponification finishes in 24-48 hours, so the soap is safe to handle after a couple of days, but uncured soap is soft, high in pH, and produces thin lather. Bramble Berry's Soap Queen blog notes cold process can be used before the full cure but will last longer and perform better with the full 4-6 weeks. Using it early will not harm you, but the bar will dissolve quickly and feel harsh on skin.

en.q: How long does hot process soap take to cure?
en.a: Hot process soap can be used sooner than cold process because the heat finishes saponification during the cook. Bramble Berry's Soap Queen blog says hot process soap can be cut within a day and is ready to use right away. The Petalmade curing guide puts it at a 1-2 week minimum cure, with about 4 weeks optimal. Hot-process bars still benefit from curing since they lose water and harden just like cold process, so it is faster but not skip-the-cure.

en.q: Does melt-and-pour soap need to cure?
en.a: No. Melt-and-pour base is already fully saponified when you buy it, so it does not require any cure time. According to Bramble Berry's Soap Queen blog, melt-and-pour does not need to cure and hardens in several hours. You only need to wait for it to set firm before unmolding and using.

en.q: Why does castile (olive oil) soap need longer to cure?
en.a: Soap high in olive oil, especially 100% olive castile, cures more slowly because olive oil is mostly soft, slow-hardening fatty acids. Lovely Greens recommends at least 6 weeks for castile, and notes that 6 months to a year produces an even harder, milder bar. Castile keeps improving long after a standard bar is done, so patience pays off.

en.q: How long does spray paint take to dry to the touch?
en.a: Most general-purpose acrylic spray paints are dry to the touch in about 20 minutes. Rust-Oleum Painter's Touch 2X and Krylon Fusion All-In-One both reach touch-dry in about 20 minutes (Krylon lists up to 25). Metallic specialty sprays take around 1 hour, and oil-based enamels like Rust-Oleum Stops Rust are only tack-free after 2-4 hours. Times assume 70°F and 50% relative humidity.

en.q: When can I apply a second coat of spray paint?
en.a: Read the label, because the recoat window is product-specific. Rust-Oleum Painter's Touch 2X should be recoated within 1 hour or after 48 hours; Stops Rust enamel within 1 hour or after 48 hours; Specialty Metallic within 1 hour or after 24 hours. Recoating during the in-between period can wrinkle or lift the first coat as its solvent re-activates.

en.q: How long until spray paint is fully cured?
en.a: Full dry takes about 24 hours, but maximum adhesion and chip resistance take longer. Rust-Oleum's plastic-bonding paints and primers state that on plastic, maximum adhesion and durability is achieved in 5-7 days, and Krylon advertises its Fusion All-In-One as fully chip resistant after 7 days. Cure is a chemical process, not just drying, so wait the full week before heavy handling, washing, or weather exposure.

en.q: Does humidity and temperature affect spray paint dry time?
en.a: Yes, heavily. Rust-Oleum allows application between 50-90°F with humidity below 65% (Krylon recommends 55-75°F and below 60%). Cool temperatures and high humidity slow solvent evaporation, lengthen every dry stage, and can cause cloudiness or a soft film. Aim for 70°F and 50% relative humidity to match the can's printed times. Always spray in a well-ventilated area.

en.q: How long do tomatoes take to grow from seed?
en.a: About 100-140 days from seed. Seeds germinate in 5-12 days at 75-85°F, seedlings grow indoors for 5-8 weeks, and then the plant needs roughly 50-90 days from transplant to first ripe fruit. Catalog "days to maturity" numbers count from transplanting, not from sowing, per Cornell and Clemson extension guidance.

en.q: How long from transplant to the first ripe tomato?
en.a: Roughly 50-90 days from transplant. Clemson Cooperative Extension gives 52-90 days depending on cultivar; the University of Maryland lists 65-90 days. Cornell groups varieties as early (65 days or fewer), mid-season (65-80), and late-season (80+) from transplant.

en.q: Are determinate or indeterminate tomatoes faster?
en.a: Determinate (bush) types are often among the faster ones, with the earliest cultivars ripening a concentrated crop in about 55-70 days from transplant. Indeterminate (vining) types range widely — some cherry types ripen in 57-60 days, while many run 70-90+ days — and they keep producing until frost. Clemson notes most early-ripening cultivars are determinate, while most heirlooms are indeterminate.

en.q: How can I make tomatoes ripen faster?
en.a: Choose a short days-to-maturity cultivar (65 days or fewer), warm the soil with black plastic two to three weeks before planting, and stake and prune indeterminates, which Cornell says can hasten the first harvest by a week or more. Keep plants in full sun (8+ hours), water evenly, and avoid excess nitrogen, which delays ripening.

en.q: How long does an avocado seed take to sprout?
en.a: Roots and a stem typically emerge 2-6 weeks after you suspend the pit in water, with the soil method giving slightly faster results. If nothing has happened by 6-8 weeks, the California Avocado Commission recommends starting over with a fresh one. The University of Nebraska Extension notes a root appears from the flat end and a shoot from the pointed end within a few weeks.

en.q: Will an avocado grown from seed produce fruit?
en.a: It can, but not reliably. UC Riverside extension experts say a seed-grown tree takes 5-13 years before it is mature enough to set fruit, and because every seed is a cross-pollinated hybrid, the fruit will NOT match the parent Hass you ate - its quality, size and taste are unpredictable. UF/IFAS adds that a seed-grown tree also lacks the parent's pest and disease resistance.

en.q: How fast does a grafted avocado tree bear fruit?
en.a: Much faster. Both UC Riverside and the California Avocado Commission say a nursery-bought grafted tree typically produces its first fruit 3-4 years after planting, because it is a cloned variety on proven rootstock rather than a genetic roll of the dice. If your goal is actually harvesting avocados, a grafted tree is the practical choice over a home-sprouted pit.

en.q: Can you get avocados from an indoor tree?
en.a: Rarely. An indoor seed-grown tree is grown mainly for its foliage - it seldom gets enough light, pollination, or size to flower and set fruit, and UC Riverside notes that avocados grow best at 60-85F and set fruit best at about 65-75F, so low light and dry indoor heat stress the plant and cause leaf drop. Treat a windowsill avocado as a leafy houseplant; for actual fruit, plant a grafted tree outdoors in a frost-free climate.

en.q: How long do potatoes take to grow from seed potatoes?
en.a: Most home-garden potato cultivars mature 90 to 120 days after planting seed pieces, per Iowa State and Maryland Extension. Early varieties finish closer to 70 to 90 days, mid-season around 90 to 110, and late storage types need 110 to 130+ days. Sprouts first emerge 14 to 28 days after planting, depending on soil temperature (Cornell).

en.q: When can I harvest new potatoes?
en.a: You can harvest small, tender new potatoes about 6 to 8 weeks (roughly 40 to 60 days) after planting, usually once the plants have flowered, according to the University of Maryland Extension. Tuber initiation begins around 55 to 70 days (IFAS), so gently dig around the hills and take just a few; new potatoes have thin skins and should be eaten within about 10 days, not stored.

en.q: What temperature and conditions do potatoes need to grow on time?
en.a: Potatoes are a cool-season crop that bulks best at 65 to 70°F. Seed pieces will not sprout until soil reaches about 40 to 45°F, and Maryland Extension warns that soil temperatures above 80°F inhibit tuber development. Give them full sun (6-plus hours), well-drained acidic soil (pH about 5.0 to 6.0), and a steady 1 inch of water per week during bulking.

en.q: How do I know when potatoes are ready to dig?
en.a: For storage potatoes, wait until the vines have fully died back, then leave tubers in the ground about two more weeks so skins toughen. Iowa State Extension suggests digging one or two test hills, if the skin rubs off easily the potatoes are immature and will not store, so wait several more days. Firm, set skins mean they are ready. For new potatoes, dig early right after flowering.

en.q: Can I use my bath towel more than 3–4 times before washing?
en.a: Only if it dries completely between uses and you are healthy. Loma Linda University environmental microbiologist Ryan Sinclair says the 3–4-use rule assumes the towel fully dries each time; if it is folded, bunched, or in a humid room, drop to 2 uses. If you have a skin infection, open wound, or weakened immune system, use a fresh towel every single time. (This is general guidance, not medical advice — follow your doctor's instructions for any active infection.)

en.q: Why does my towel smell musty even after I wash it?
en.a: That sour smell comes from volatile organic compounds produced by bacteria and mold that survived in the damp fabric. It means bacteria multiplied before the wash or that the towel was left damp too long. Rewash in the hottest water the label allows, dry fully, and going forward spread towels open and run the bathroom fan so they dry between uses.

en.q: How often should you wash kitchen towels?
en.a: Daily. Michigan State University Extension advises changing cloth kitchen towels every day because they touch raw food, juices, dirty hands, and counters, making them a major cross-contamination risk. FoodSafety.gov also recommends washing dishcloths often in the hot cycle of your washing machine.

en.q: How often should you wash hand towels?
en.a: Hand towels follow the same rule as bath towels — every 3 to 4 uses, or at least once a week. Houston Methodist dermatologist Dr. Jennifer Maender recommends laundering both bath and hand towels after every three uses, and Cleveland Clinic likewise puts them on the same weekly cycle. Because hand towels get touched by many hands throughout the day, a busy or sick household should swap them more often — every day or two in those cases.

en.q: Can a mattress really last 20 years?
en.a: Only a premium natural latex mattress can plausibly reach the 20-year mark — Saatva and other manufacturers quote 10–20 years for latex, with some models built for 15-plus. Every other type tops out closer to 8–10 years. Twenty years is realistic solely for high-quality latex that is rotated and protected; expecting it from foam, hybrid, or innerspring beds is unrealistic.

en.q: How often should you replace a mattress?
en.a: Sleep Foundation recommends replacing every 6 to 8 years under normal conditions, and the Better Sleep Council uses a 7-year rule of thumb as the point to start comparing new models. Replace sooner if you notice sagging, feel springs, sleep worse than in hotels, or wake with new aches and stiffness. Age is a guideline; the warning signs are the real trigger.

en.q: What are the signs a mattress is worn out?
en.a: According to Sleep Foundation and the Better Sleep Council, the clearest signs are visible sagging or permanent body impressions, noisy or poking springs, waking with back or joint stiffness, sleeping better away from home, and a noticeable rise in allergy or asthma symptoms — old mattresses accumulate dust mites and other allergens. Visible rips, lumps, or being 7+ years old also mean it's time.

en.q: How can I make my mattress last longer?
en.a: Rotate it every 3 months (flip too, if the maker allows), use a mattress protector to block sweat and mites, keep it on a solid or properly slatted foundation — never the floor, which can void the warranty — and vacuum or spot-clean it regularly. Pair it with fresh sheets washed weekly and pillows replaced every 1–2 years so grime doesn't migrate into the bed.

en.q: How long do pillows last on average?
en.a: Most experts recommend replacing pillows every 1 to 2 years, according to the Sleep Foundation. The exact lifespan depends on the fill: polyester lasts 6 months to 2 years, down alternative 1 to 2 years, memory foam and polyfoam 2 to 3 years, and latex 2 to 4 years. The Asthma and Allergy Foundation of America specifically recommends every 2 years for allergy sufferers because pillows accumulate dust mites and dead skin.

en.q: How long does a memory foam pillow last?
en.a: Memory foam pillows last about 2 to 3 years on average, per the Sleep Foundation. Premium high-density memory foam can last longer; Tempur-Pedic backs its memory-foam pillows with a 5-year limited warranty against cell-structure deterioration that stops the pillow returning to its original shape. That warranty covers defects, not the gradual softening that usually prompts replacement.

en.q: What is the pillow fold test?
en.a: Fold the pillow in half, squeeze out the air, and let go. The Sleep Foundation says a down or feather pillow should spring back to its normal shape on its own; if it stays folded or recovers slowly, the fill has lost resilience and the pillow should be replaced. For foam pillows, press the center firmly and look for a lingering dent.

en.q: How often should you replace pillows for allergies?
en.a: The Asthma and Allergy Foundation of America recommends replacing pillows every 2 years if you have dust-mite allergies, because they collect dead skin cells and dust mites over time. The American Lung Association notes the average person sheds 1.5 grams of skin flakes daily, enough to feed a million dust mites, and those flakes concentrate in pillows. Using allergen-proof encasements between replacements helps. This is general allergen-hygiene guidance, not medical advice; for persistent symptoms, talk to a doctor or allergist.

en.q: How often should a newborn eat in a 24-hour period?
en.a: A newborn should eat 8 to 12 times every 24 hours, roughly every 2 to 3 hours around the clock, according to the AAP. Breastfed babies tend toward the higher end (10-12 feeds); bottle-fed babies usually manage closer to 8. The WHO recommends feeding on demand, day and night. Frequency is guided by early hunger cues rather than a strict clock. This is general guidance, not medical advice; talk to your pediatrician about your baby's specific needs.

en.q: How many ounces should a newborn eat per feeding?
en.a: Per AAP guidance, newborns take about half an ounce per feed in the first 1-2 days, then 1-2 ounces after the first few days. By the end of the first month, most babies take 3-4 ounces every 3-4 hours. Breastfed intake can't be measured directly, so track wet diapers, stools, and weight gain instead of volume.

en.q: Is it normal for a newborn to eat every hour?
en.a: Yes, during cluster feeding. La Leche League explains that newborns may bunch several feeds into a few hours, then sleep a longer stretch. This is normal and typically happens during growth spurts — commonly around 7-10 days and between 3-6 weeks, recurring several times in the first 3 months — lasting 2-3 days. Frequent feeding signals your body to increase milk supply.

en.q: How do I know my newborn is getting enough milk?
en.a: Per La Leche League GB, look for 6+ heavy wet diapers and at least 3 yellow, seedy stools per day after the first few days, plus contentment after most feeds and steady weight gain (regaining birth weight by about 2 weeks, then about an ounce per day). If output drops, weight gain stalls, or your baby is lethargic, contact your pediatrician or a lactation consultant promptly.

en.q: How long do newborns sleep at night?
en.a: Newborns do not yet have a 'night' — they sleep roughly 14 to 17 hours per 24 hours scattered fairly evenly across day and night, in stretches of 1 to 4 hours. In the earliest weeks a single nighttime block is typically just 1 to 2 hours, lengthening toward 4 hours by 8 to 12 weeks as the circadian rhythm develops. The longest medically expected stretch is about 4 hours between feeds.

en.q: When do newborns start sleeping through the night?
en.a: Most newborns are not developmentally able to sleep a long nighttime stretch until 3 to 6 months. The AAP notes that regular sleep cycles do not organize until roughly 6 months. From 8 to 12 weeks many babies begin one longer 4 to 6 hour nighttime block, but 'sleeping through the night' for a young infant is often defined as just a 5 to 6 hour stretch, not an adult 8-hour stretch.

en.q: How long can a newborn stay awake between naps?
en.a: A newborn's wake window is short — roughly 30 to 60 minutes in the first month, lengthening to 1 to 2 hours (60 to 120 minutes) from 1 to 3 months, per Cleveland Clinic. Watch for early tired cues (yawning, staring, red eyebrows) and start the wind-down before fussing begins; an overtired newborn actually sleeps less, not more.

en.q: Why does my newborn sleep all day and stay up at night?
en.a: This is day-night confusion, which HealthyChildren.org describes as normal for newborns: they sleep through the day and demand feeds and interaction at night because their circadian rhythm has not yet developed. Use bright light and normal noise during the day and dim, quiet interactions at night. It usually resolves on its own over the first few months as the circadian rhythm matures.

en.q: When does the 4 month sleep regression start?
en.a: It usually begins around 3 to 4 months of age, sometimes a few weeks earlier or later. The timing lines up with the moment a baby's brain begins moving through the four adult-like sleep stages instead of the two newborn stages, which the AAP notes happens as regular sleep cycles develop around 4 to 6 months.

en.q: How long does the 4 month sleep regression last?
en.a: Most families see it resolve within a few days to a few weeks, often within a week or two. The Sleep Foundation notes the disruption can be as short as a few days for some babies, while others take a few weeks. The biological change is permanent; only the disrupted period is temporary.

en.q: Why does the 4 month sleep regression happen?
en.a: It happens because sleep permanently matures. Newborns have just two sleep stages (active/REM and quiet/NREM), but around 3 to 4 months babies begin cycling through four adult-like stages, each cycle running well under an hour with a brief partial waking at the end. Learning to link those cycles is the regression.

en.q: When should I talk to a pediatrician about the sleep regression?
en.a: Check in if sleep has not improved after several weeks, is getting worse, or comes with fewer than 5 to 6 wet diapers a day, poor weight gain, fever, persistent crying, breathing changes, snoring, gasping, or pauses in breathing. This guide is general information, not medical advice - your pediatrician knows your baby's individual history.

en.q: Can a spacecraft reach Pluto faster than 9.5 years?
en.a: Not with today's standard rockets. New Horizons already set the record for the fastest launch ever — about 36,400 mph — and used a Jupiter gravity assist that NASA says shaved three years off the trip. Matching that ~9.5-year timeline again would require a similarly fast launch and a well-timed Jupiter window. Going faster would need new propulsion technology; slowing to orbit would take decades. (NASA, New Horizons)

en.q: Why did New Horizons fly past Pluto instead of orbiting it?
en.a: Speed. To reach Pluto in about nine years, New Horizons had to travel faster than 30,000 mph — far too fast to be captured by tiny Pluto's weak gravity. Slowing into orbit would have required carrying massive braking fuel reserves, which would have made the spacecraft heavier and the trip much longer. NASA therefore chose a fast flyby, brief but actually achievable, over an impractical orbiter. (NASA)

en.q: How long does a radio signal take to reach Pluto?
en.a: About 4.5 to 5.5 hours one way, depending on where Pluto is in its orbit. NASA notes that sunlight itself takes roughly 5.5 hours to travel from the Sun to Pluto at its average distance of 39 AU. That communications lag is why New Horizons had to execute its 2015 flyby autonomously — commands from Earth were hours out of date by the time they arrived. (NASA, Pluto Facts)

en.q: How far away is Pluto?
en.a: Pluto averages about 3.7 billion miles (5.9 billion km) from the Sun — roughly 39 AU, or 39 times the Earth–Sun distance. Its elliptical orbit swings it between about 30 AU at its closest and 49 AU at its farthest. New Horizons covered more than 3 billion miles to reach it. That enormous distance, plus the speed needed to cross it, is what makes the trip take years. (NASA)

en.q: How long does a SpaceX Crew Dragon take to reach the ISS?
en.a: A Crew Dragon typically docks about one day after launch, with recent missions ranging from roughly 15 to 28 hours. The exact time depends on the phasing plan; NASA prioritizes a careful, well-instrumented approach over raw speed because the roomier cabin makes the longer ride comfortable for the crew.

en.q: Why did Soyuz trips to the ISS used to take two days?
en.a: Early Soyuz and many Progress cargo flights used a classic two-day, roughly 34-orbit profile that slowly raised the chaser's orbit until it matched the station's. It was simpler and safer, and for uncrewed cargo it remains common. Improved guidance and Baikonur's favorable latitude later enabled the six-hour fast-track, introduced in 2013, and the three-hour ultrafast profile.

en.q: How far away is the ISS, and isn't that close enough to reach fast?
en.a: The ISS orbits at about 408 km (250 miles) up, genuinely close in cosmic terms. The challenge is that the station moves at about 28,000 km/h (17,500 mph), so a craft can't fly straight to it. It must launch into the same orbital plane and chase the station down, which is why even a near neighbor takes hours to reach.

en.q: What is the fastest anyone has ever reached the ISS?
en.a: The confirmed record is 3 hours and 3 minutes from launch to docking, set by Russia's Soyuz MS-17 on October 14, 2020, and verified by Guinness World Records. Using an ultrafast two-orbit rendezvous, the capsule climbed to meet the station over about two and a half orbits.

en.q: Does sunlight take exactly 8 minutes to reach Earth?
en.a: Not exactly — about 8 minutes 20 seconds (499 seconds, or 8.317 minutes) on average. Because Earth’s orbit is elliptical, the real time ranges from roughly 8 minutes 10 seconds at perihelion (closest, early January) to 8 minutes 27 seconds at aphelion (farthest, early July). The familiar “8 minutes” is a rounded figure NASA uses for simplicity.

en.q: How long does light take to reach Earth from the Moon and other planets?
en.a: From the Moon, about 1.28 seconds. Sunlight reaches Jupiter in about 43.2 minutes and Pluto in roughly 5.5 hours. A signal from Mars takes about 3 minutes at closest approach to roughly 22 minutes at the planets’ farthest separation — one reason NASA rovers can’t be driven in real time.

en.q: What speed does light travel at, and why is 299,792 km/s the limit?
en.a: Light moves at 299,792,458 meters per second (about 186,000 miles or 300,000 km per second) in a vacuum — a fixed constant under Einstein’s relativity and the universe’s ultimate speed limit for energy and information. No signal, including radio or laser communications, can travel faster.

en.q: If the Sun went out, how long until we would notice?
en.a: About 8 minutes 20 seconds. Because light and all of the Sun’s radiation travel at the finite speed of light, we would continue to see the Sun and receive its energy for roughly 500 seconds after it actually disappeared — a striking illustration that we always see the Sun as it was, not as it is.

en.q: What is the absolute best month to visit Italy?
en.a: May or October. Daytime highs in Rome are a comfortable 22–24°C (72–75°F), crowds are thinner than in summer, prices are lower than the July–August peak, and almost everything is open. May gives blooming countryside and empty beaches; October brings autumn foliage, the grape and olive harvests, and truffle festivals.

en.q: What is the cheapest time to visit Italy?
en.a: November through February, excluding the Christmas-to-Epiphany holidays (around 24 December to 6 January) and the ski resorts. City hotels and flights drop to their lowest rates, museums such as the Uffizi are at their quietest, and headline sights are uncrowded. The trade-off is shorter days and many coastal hotels and restaurants closing until Easter.

en.q: When should you avoid visiting Italy?
en.a: August is the toughest month for most travellers: it is the hottest, most crowded and most expensive time, and because of the Ferragosto holiday on 15 August many city restaurants and shops shut while Italians flood the coast. Temperatures in the cities and south regularly exceed 35°C (95°F). Also avoid the Easter week and late June–July in the major cities if sightseeing is your main goal.

en.q: When is the best time to visit the Italian coast and beaches?
en.a: Roughly May to September, when the sea is warm enough to swim and coastal towns are fully open. Late May, June and September are ideal – warm water with far smaller crowds than August. The Amalfi Coast, Cinque Terre, Sardinia, Sicily and Puglia all follow this pattern; book well ahead for July and August.

en.q: What is the best month to visit Spain?
en.a: May is widely considered the single best month: temperatures sit around 16–24°C, rainfall is low (Seville sees roughly 30 mm all month per AEMET), and crowds and prices are still below the summer peak. April, June, September and October are close runners-up.

en.q: What is the cheapest time to visit Spain?
en.a: November through February is the cheapest window, when flights and hotels drop to their lowest levels — Lonely Planet calls it "the best time for budget travelers." Late January and February tend to be the lowest-priced weeks, and Spain's winter rebajas (sales) run January–February with discounts up to 70% off.

en.q: Is August a bad time to visit Spain?
en.a: For most travelers, yes. Central and southern Spain regularly exceed 40°C (104°F) in August, Madrid empties out as locals flee the heat, and the coasts hit peak crowds and peak prices. The exceptions are the northern coast (Galicia, Asturias, Basque Country), which stays mild, and specific festivals like La Tomatina.

en.q: When can you ski in Spain?
en.a: Ski resorts generally open in December and close just after Easter. Peak snow runs January to March in the Pyrenees, January to February in central Spain, and the Sierra Nevada near Granada sometimes stays open until May, allowing a ski-and-beach combination in the same day.

en.q: What is the absolute best month to visit Paris?
en.a: The single best window is April to June or September to October. Lonely Planet's Paris authors single out spring (especially April–May) and autumn (especially September–October) for thinner crowds and temperate, lovely weather. Paris daytime highs reach about 16°C in April, ~23°C in June, and 22°C in September (Météo-France, Paris-Orly 1991–2020 normals). If you must pick one month, choose May or September for the best weather-to-crowd ratio.

en.q: When is the cheapest time to visit France?
en.a: The cheapest time is winter, roughly November through February, excluding the Christmas and New Year holidays. Lonely Planet names December to January as the best budget window for Paris, when sights are quieter and prices lower. There is also a cheaper pocket in August in Paris itself, when hotel rates often drop as locals leave for vacation — though many restaurants and shops shut, so you trade savings for closures.

en.q: Is August a bad time to visit Paris?
en.a: August is a mixed bag. On the upside, Paris empties of locals, traffic is lighter, and hotel rates are often at their lowest. On the downside, temperatures average around 26°C (Météo-France) and many restaurants, small shops, and some services shut for the month as Parisians take their vacations — Lonely Planet warns it can be hard to get a good bistro meal. It is not the worst time, but if classic café culture matters to you, choose spring or September instead.

en.q: When is the best time to visit the French Riviera and the Alps?
en.a: For the Côte d'Azur, the best beach season runs May to September; Nice averages about 28°C in August with sea temperatures near 24°C (Météo-France, Nice 1991–2020), but for fewer crowds target May, June, or September. For the Alps, ski season runs December to March (into April at altitude) — larger high resorts like Les Trois Vallées open from early-to-mid December through mid-April, while lower resorts may only run mid-January to mid-March depending on snow.

en.q: When is the best time to visit Greece?
en.a: The best time to visit Greece is mid-May through June and September. The islands are fully open, the sea is warm enough for swimming, daylight is long, crowds are thinner than in peak summer, and prices sit below the July-August high. If you can pick only one month, choose September, when the sea is at its warmest and school holidays are over.

en.q: What is the cheapest time to visit Greece?
en.a: The cheapest time is the off-season from November to March, when airfares, ferry prices and hotel rates drop steeply. Between 1 November and 31 March the state also reduces entrance fees at ancient sites and state museums, making an Athens city break very affordable. For a cheap but still swimmable beach trip, aim for late September or October.

en.q: When is the worst time to visit Greece?
en.a: There is no outright bad time, but late July and August disappoint travellers who dislike heat and crowds: it is the hottest, driest period (July and August are the hottest months, with average highs around 32-33C) and the busiest, with peak prices. The depth of winter (January-February) is also weak for an island beach holiday, since the sea is cold, many island businesses shut, and ferry schedules are skeletal.

en.q: When are the Greek islands open and ferries running?
en.a: The island-hopping season unofficially opens with Orthodox Easter in April or May (12 April 2026; 2 May 2027) and runs through October, with most hotels closing by the end of October. In the off-season (November to March) many small-island hotels and restaurants shut down and ferries that run daily in summer may drop to two or three sailings a week. Larger islands such as Crete, Rhodes, Corfu and Kefalonia stay more active year-round.

en.q: What is the best month to visit Switzerland for hiking?
en.a: Mid-June to mid-September is the best window for hiking, when daytime highs reach 18-28°C (65-82°F) and the high alpine passes and cable cars are open. July and August are the warmest but also the most crowded and expensive; mid-June and September offer similar conditions with far fewer people on the trails.

en.q: When is ski season in Switzerland?
en.a: The main ski season runs from December to March. January and February are the coldest and most snow-reliable, while the Christmas/New Year period and February school holidays are the busiest and priciest. Resorts also maintain more than 5,000 km of cross-country trails, and you can check current snow depth on the official Swiss snow report before you go.

en.q: What is the cheapest time to visit Switzerland?
en.a: The shoulder periods of April-May and October-November are the cheapest, with lower flights, hotels and thinner crowds than summer. November is the lowest-priced month of all, though it brings foggy lowlands and some 'between-seasons' closures. For a balance of decent weather and lower cost, target mid-June or September.

en.q: When should I avoid visiting Switzerland?
en.a: Switzerland's climate is moderate year-round, so no month is truly unvisitable. But if you dislike crowds, avoid mid-July to mid-August; if you do not ski, avoid the Christmas/New Year and February peaks, when ski resorts are packed and expensive. November is the quietest month but also the greyest, with low cloud over the plateau and several mountain hotels closed for the season.

en.q: What is the absolute best month to visit London?
en.a: July is the warmest and sunniest month, averaging a high of 23.9°C with about 218 hours of sunshine, and it hosts Wimbledon and Pride. For slightly fewer crowds with near-peak weather, June and September are excellent alternatives; for the best value-for-conditions balance, May is the sweet spot.

en.q: When is the cheapest time to visit London / UK?
en.a: January and February are the cheapest months, when flights, hotels and attractions drop to their lowest prices after Christmas. Early March and late October-November also offer shoulder-season value with noticeably better weather than midwinter. Avoid mid-December through New Year, when festive demand pushes rates back up.

en.q: What is the worst time to visit London?
en.a: For weather, November to February is the toughest window - cold, wet (November is the wettest month at around 67 mm of rain) and dark, with only about eight hours of daylight in December. If your priority is avoiding crowds rather than cold, peak July-August is the worst time for you because of packed transport, long queues and peak pricing.

en.q: How many days do you need in London?
en.a: Four to five days is enough to cover London's headline sights - the Tower of London, British Museum, Westminster, a West End show and a couple of major galleries - at a comfortable pace. Allow a full week if you want day trips (Windsor, Bath, Stonehenge, Oxford or Cambridge) or to explore neighbourhoods like Shoreditch, Notting Hill and Greenwich in depth.

en.q: What is the absolute best month to visit Amsterdam?
en.a: Mid-to-late April is the standout: the tulips are at peak bloom, King's Day (April 27) brings the year's biggest street party, days are mild (around 15C/59F average high), and prices have not yet hit summer levels. If you prefer fewer crowds, September is the runner-up, with lingering warmth, lighter footfall, and festivals like Amsterdam Fashion Week.

en.q: When is tulip season in the Netherlands?
en.a: Tulip season runs roughly mid-March to mid-May. Keukenhof, the famous spring garden in Lisse, opens for about eight weeks inside that window (it ran March 19 to May 10 in 2026). For the open bulb fields at their most colourful, target mid-April to early May; exact timing depends on the weather each spring.

en.q: What is the cheapest time to visit Amsterdam?
en.a: February is typically the cheapest month, falling just before tulip season begins. Hotels and flights hit their lowest prices and museums are at their emptiest. January is similarly cheap. For a better balance of low prices and tolerable weather, March (before the bloom rush) and October are the value picks.

en.q: Is Amsterdam worth visiting in winter?
en.a: Yes, if you pack for it. Winter averages a mild 3C (37F), rarely freezing hard, and you get the lowest prices of the year, the Amsterdam Light Festival, Christmas markets, and ice-skating rinks. The trade-off is grey, short days with little sunshine (around 55-67 sunshine hours in December and January). Bring warm layers and waterproof shoes.

en.q: What is the best month to visit Thailand?
en.a: The best months are November through February, during Thailand's cool, dry season. December and January offer the most comfortable weather, with daytime highs around 28 to 31C and low humidity, but they are also the busiest and most expensive. November and February are excellent shoulder months with similar conditions and slightly fewer crowds.

en.q: When is the cheapest time to visit Thailand?
en.a: The cheapest time to visit is the late monsoon, from September to October, when crowds and prices hit their annual lows and you rarely need to book ahead. May through July is a good-value middle ground, especially on the Andaman coast (Phuket, Krabi), where resorts offer large discounts and rains are usually brief.

en.q: When should I avoid visiting Thailand?
en.a: Avoid March through May if you are sensitive to heat, as Bangkok has recently hit 40C (104F) and northern Thailand regularly reaches 36C (97F). Avoid September and October if you want to escape heavy rain and any flooding risk, particularly in the north and northeast, which can occasionally affect riverside areas of Bangkok.

en.q: Which Thai islands are best during the rainy season?
en.a: The Gulf of Thailand islands (Ko Samui, Ko Phangan, and Ko Tao) have a different weather pattern from the Andaman coast and actually hit their peak season in July and August. If you are traveling during the European summer, the Gulf islands are the smart choice, while the Andaman coast (Phuket, Krabi) is quieter, wetter, and much cheaper at that time.

en.q: What is the best month to visit Bali?
en.a: The best months are May, June and July, when the dry season is in full swing, humidity is lower, rainfall is minimal and the peak holiday crowds of August have not yet peaked. September is also outstanding if you want similar weather at lower prices, as it is a shoulder month.

en.q: When is the rainy season in Bali?
en.a: Bali's wet (rainy) season runs from November to March, driven by the northwest monsoon. January and February are typically the wettest months, each receiving around 280–350 mm of rain. Showers are often heavy but short, and the island stays warm (around 27–28°C).

en.q: What is the cheapest time to visit Bali?
en.a: The cheapest time is the low season — January to March and November — when rains keep crowds away and hotels and flights drop to their lowest rates. You will trade some sunshine for big savings and a quieter island, though the east coast still offers decent surf.

en.q: Is Bali warm enough to visit year-round?
en.a: Yes. Bali sits about 8 degrees south of the equator, so temperatures stay between roughly 28°C and 32°C (82–90°F) all year with close to 12 hours of daylight. It only gets noticeably cooler in the central mountains, where Mount Agung rises above 3,000 metres and is wetter and colder than the coast.

en.q: What is the absolute best month to visit New York City?
en.a: May is widely considered the best single month to visit New York City—Lonely Planet calls it "perhaps the best month for New York City weather." Average highs reach about 71°F (22°C) with low humidity, the cherry blossoms are fading into full green, Broadway rolls out new shows ahead of the Tony Awards, and outdoor dining is in full swing. October is the close runner-up for fall foliage and crisp, scenic days.

en.q: What is the cheapest time to visit New York City?
en.a: January through early March (skipping holiday weekends) is the cheapest time to visit. Once the Christmas rush clears, hotel rates fall to their lowest of the year, and crowds thin out. You trade mild weather for cold—Central Park averages 8.8" of snow in January and 10.1" in February—but you'll save significantly on lodging and attractions.

en.q: When should you avoid visiting New York City?
en.a: Avoid late July through mid-August if you dislike heat, humidity, high prices, and heavy crowds. July is the hottest (average high 85°F/29°C), most humid, and most expensive month, with the most rainfall of the year. Also watch the forecast in September and early October, when rare hurricane remnants can bring a rainy day or two, though direct hurricane hits on NYC are uncommon.

en.q: Is December a good time to visit New York City?
en.a: December is magical but expensive and cold. The Rockefeller Center Christmas tree, Bryant Park holiday market, Fifth Avenue window displays, and ice rinks make it one of the most festive cities in the world—but hotel prices "skyrocket to summertime levels," days are short (sunset near 4:30pm), and average highs only reach about 44°F (7°C). Go for the atmosphere, just book early and budget accordingly.

en.q: How long do pet snakes live on average?
en.a: Most pet snakes live 10–30+ years, with popular beginner species averaging about 15–25 years in captivity. Corn snakes typically reach ~15–20 years, ball pythons ~20–30 years, and boas 25–35 years, while smaller species like garter snakes average closer to 6–10 years.

en.q: Which pet snake lives the longest?
en.a: Among common pet species, boas and pythons live the longest. Boa constrictors typically reach 25–35 years with a documented record of 40 years, and ball pythons average 20–30 years with a record near 50 years (reported by the Philadelphia Zoo). In general, boas and pythons outlive colubrids like corn snakes and kingsnakes.

en.q: How long do snakes live in the wild versus captivity?
en.a: Captive snakes live considerably longer than wild ones. Garter snakes average only about 2 years in the wild versus 6–10 in captivity, and boas average roughly 20 years in the wild versus 25–35 in captivity. Predation, disease, starvation, and exposure are largely removed in captivity, which is why good husbandry is the biggest factor in a pet snake's lifespan.

en.q: How can I help my snake live longer?
en.a: Provide a proper heat gradient (cool end 70–75°F, warm end 90–95°F), species-appropriate humidity (often 40–70%), whole frozen-thawed prey on the right schedule, safe substrate, secure hides, and a clean enclosure. Quarantine new animals, and work with a reptile veterinarian for check-ups and any signs of illness such as anorexia, wheezing, or poor sheds. This is general care information, not veterinary advice; a snake that is gasping/open-mouth breathing, weak or flaccid, twisted, or non-responsive is an emergency—see an exotics veterinarian immediately.

en.q: How long do pet chinchillas live on average?
en.a: Pet chinchillas typically live 10–15 years, with the upper range reaching about 20 years in captivity, according to the Merck Veterinary Manual. That makes them one of the longest-lived rodents kept as pets. With excellent diet, cool housing, and routine exotic-vet care, many well-kept chinchillas live into their mid-teens.

en.q: What is the oldest recorded chinchilla lifespan?
en.a: Verified longevity records are more modest than internet rumors. The AnAge longevity database lists a formal captive maximum of 17.2 years (Weigl, 2005), while Animal Diversity Web notes that some domesticated chinchillas have lived for more than 20 years (Nowak, 1999, unconfirmed). Claims of chinchillas reaching 29 years circulate online, but they are not confirmed by formal longevity registries.

en.q: What is the most common cause of death in chinchillas?
en.a: Among preventable causes, heat stroke is one of the most common and deadly, because chinchillas are very sensitive to heat and humidity (keep housing below 80°F, ideally 55–68°F). Dental disease—found in roughly one-third of apparently healthy chinchillas per the Merck Veterinary Manual—and gastrointestinal stasis from poor diet or sudden food changes are also leading causes of illness and death. This is general information, not veterinary advice; a chinchilla that stops eating, pants in a warm room, drools, or shows labored breathing is in a potential emergency and should see an exotic veterinarian immediately.

en.q: Do male and female chinchillas live different lengths of time?
en.a: There is no well-documented, significant lifespan difference between male and female chinchillas. Sex-specific risks do exist, however: intact males can develop a 'fur ring' (hair constricting the penis) that causes urinary retention, and breeding females face birth-related risks. Spaying/neutering decisions should be made with an exotic veterinarian, but sex itself is not a major driver of overall lifespan.

en.q: How long do axolotls live as pets?
en.a: Pet axolotls typically live 10 to 15 years in captivity when kept in cool (60-64F / 16-18C), clean, well-cycled water and fed a carnivorous diet of worms and pellets. The 15-year mark represents well-cared-for animals; neglected ones can die within months. This is care information, not veterinary advice; if your axolotl is unwell, consult an exotic-animal vet.

en.q: How long do axolotls live in the wild?
en.a: Wild axolotls have a potential lifespan of about 10 to 15 years, but very few reach it. The species is critically endangered, with National Geographic and Wikipedia estimating only around 50 to 1,000 adult individuals left in the canals of Lake Xochimilco, where pollution, invasive fish, and habitat loss kill most before old age.

en.q: What is the oldest an axolotl can live?
en.a: The commonly cited upper limit for a captive axolotl is about 15 years, reported by zoos and veterinary sources. Laboratory animals average much shorter lives, around 5 to 6 years, because of research use and post-metamorphosis mortality.

en.q: Do male or female axolotls live longer?
en.a: There is no well-documented sex difference in axolotl lifespan; males and females generally live about the same 10 to 15 years in captivity. Care factors such as water temperature, water quality, diet, and disease matter far more than sex in determining how long an individual lives.

en.q: How long do leopard geckos live as pets?
en.a: Most pet leopard geckos live 10-15 years with basic care, and well-cared-for individuals often reach 15-20 years. The documented captive maximum sits around 22 years (Animal Diversity Web), making them one of the longest-lived lizards for their size. Exceptional individuals may live longer still, though reliable figures cluster around two decades.

en.q: How long do leopard geckos live in the wild?
en.a: Wild leopard geckos live far shorter lives than captive ones-often only several years. Predation, parasites, irregular food, and temperature extremes all cut their lives short. There is no robust field longevity dataset, which is why trustworthy numbers come from protected captive animals rather than wild populations.

en.q: Do leopard geckos need UVB light to live a long life?
en.a: It is debated. Merck lists UVB as having 'no special requirement' for leopard geckos, while VCA Animal Hospitals recommends it. Because UVB drives the vitamin D3 that lets geckos absorb calcium, most keepers now provide low-level UVB mounted 10-12 inches away as inexpensive insurance against metabolic bone disease. This is general husbandry information, not veterinary advice-consult a reptile veterinarian about your specific setup.

en.q: What is the most common reason leopard geckos die early?
en.a: Poor calcium and vitamin D3-leading to metabolic bone disease (MBD)-is one of the most common preventable causes of illness and early death; Merck calls MBD 'the most common bone disease encountered in reptile practice.' Close behind are intestinal impaction from unsafe substrate (loose sand, walnut shell, gravel) and parasitic infections such as Cryptosporidium. All three are largely preventable with correct diet, safe substrate, and routine fecal testing. This is general care information, not veterinary advice-see a reptile veterinarian promptly if your gecko stops eating, loses weight rapidly, develops a swollen jaw or limbs, trembles, or has persistent diarrhea.

en.q: How long do hermit crabs live as pets?
en.a: With proper care, pet hermit crabs typically live 10 to 15 years or more, with a peer-reviewed longevity record of about 12 years for the Caribbean species (Coenobita clypeatus). However, most captive crabs die within their first one to two years because of poor habitat — low humidity, shallow substrate, or missing salt water — rather than old age.

en.q: Can hermit crabs really live 30 or 40 years?
en.a: Owner-reported claims of 30- to 40-year-old hermit crabs exist in the hobbyist community, but they have not been scientifically verified. Treat these figures as the outer ceiling of what is possible rather than the norm. The only formally documented lifespan is roughly 12 years, recorded in a peer-reviewed study of Coenobita clypeatus.

en.q: Why do most pet hermit crabs die so young?
en.a: The leading causes of early death are environmental: humidity below the required 70–85%, temperatures outside the 75–85°F range, substrate too shallow for safe molting, lack of marine-grade salt water, and poor diet. Hermit crabs breathe through modified gills that must stay moist, so a dry tank effectively suffocates them over time.

en.q: Do hermit crabs from pet stores breed in captivity?
en.a: No. Land hermit crabs do not breed in human care at any commercial scale because their larvae must develop in the open ocean. Essentially every crab sold in a pet shop was harvested from the wild, which is why the trade is considered unsustainable and why a captive crab's remaining lifespan is so hard to predict.

en.q: Does unopened perfume expire?
en.a: Unopened perfume doesn't expire on a fixed date, because U.S. fragrance has no regulated expiration. But it does slowly degrade. Expect about 3-5 years of good quality when the bottle is sealed and kept cool and dark; dense woody or oriental formulas can last longer, while citrus scents age fastest. These are perfumer-consensus estimates, not legal expiry dates.

en.q: How long does perfume last on skin?
en.a: Roughly 3-12 hours, set by concentration. A pure parfum (20-30% oils) can last 6-12+ hours, eau de parfum about 4-8 hours, eau de toilette 3-5 hours, and eau de cologne around 2 hours. These tiers are long-standing perfumery convention and ranges overlap; skin chemistry, hydration, and where you apply (pulse points) also affect wear time.

en.q: How should I store perfume to make it last?
en.a: Keep it cool, dark, and sealed - ideally in the original box in a bedroom drawer or closet, not a humid bathroom. Avoid sunlight, heat, and temperature swings, and decant half-empty bottles into smaller airtight sprays to limit the oxygen headspace above the liquid.

en.q: Can expired perfume irritate skin?
en.a: Yes. Citrus and floral terpenes like limonene and linalool oxidize when exposed to air, forming hydroperoxides that are strong contact allergens. If a fragrance causes redness, itching, or swelling, stop using it and see a doctor; for throat or face swelling, trouble breathing, or dizziness, seek emergency care. This is general health information, not medical advice.

en.q: How long does permanent hair dye last?
en.a: Permanent (oxidative) dye colors the hair permanently, so it has to grow out. Roots usually become visible about 4-6 weeks after coloring, and most people re-touch around 6-8 weeks. The dyed length itself can hold its tone for months, though it fades and shifts over time (He et al., 2022).

en.q: How many washes does semi-permanent or demi-permanent hair dye last?
en.a: Demi-permanent typically lasts about 12-24 washes, and semi-permanent about 8-12 washes. Peer-reviewed reviews use a slightly different three-way split, reporting their temporary-dye category at ~8-12 washings and their semi-permanent category at ~24 washes, because the exact count depends on porosity, shade depth, and wash habits (He et al., 2022).

en.q: What makes hair dye fade faster?
en.a: Frequent washing (especially with hot water and sulfate shampoos) is the biggest factor, because research shows dye leaches out of the hair shaft over multiple wash cycles (Zhang et al., 2016). Sunlight/UV, high-heat styling, hard-water minerals, chlorine, and porous, damaged hair also speed fading.

en.q: How long does a hair-dye allergic reaction last, and when is it an emergency?
en.a: Mild allergic contact dermatitis usually settles over several days once the allergen (often PPD in permanent dye) is removed, though severe cases take longer and sensitization is usually lifelong (DermNet NZ). Reactions are typically delayed, appearing 24-72 hours after exposure. Go to emergency care for face or throat swelling, trouble breathing or swallowing, a fast-spreading rash, eye involvement, or dizziness, as these can signal anaphylaxis. This is health information, not medical advice; see a doctor for any reaction.

en.q: How long does opened wine last in the fridge?
en.a: Once resealed and refrigerated, sparkling wine lasts 1-2 days, light whites and rosés 3-5 days, full-bodied reds 3-6 days, and fortified wines like port 1-3 weeks. A dedicated sparkling stopper can stretch bubbles to about 2-3 days.

en.q: How long does unopened wine last?
en.a: Stored cool and dark, everyday whites keep about 1-2 years past their printed date, reds 2-3 years, non-vintage sparkling 3-4 years, and vintage sparkling 5-10 years. Fine wine can age 10-20+ years, and fortified wines like port and Madeira can last decades.

en.q: Does wine go bad, and is spoiled wine dangerous?
en.a: Yes. Wine spoils through oxidation and microbial growth, showing as brown color, a vinegar or burnt-rubber smell, or a sharp sour taste. A sip rarely causes harm, but heavily spoiled wine can trigger food-poisoning symptoms like upset stomach, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, and fever. This is health information, not medical advice - see a doctor if symptoms are severe or persistent, or include dehydration, a high fever, or blood in vomit or stool.

en.q: How should you store wine to make it last longer?
en.a: Keep unopened bottles cool (around 55°F/13°C), dark, and steady in temperature, lying on their side at about 60% humidity so the cork stays moist. Wine tolerates up to about 69°F (21°C) fine, but sustained heat above roughly 77°F (25°C) can spoil it. Once open, re-cork tightly and refrigerate (even reds), minimize the air gap, and use a vacuum or sparkling stopper to slow oxidation.

en.q: How long does caffeine last in your system?
en.a: Caffeine has an average half-life of about 5 hours, with a normal range of 1.5 to 9.5 hours depending on genetics, pregnancy, medications, and liver function. After 5 hours roughly half is still in your bloodstream, after 10 hours about a quarter remains, and it takes about 24-25 hours (around 5 half-lives) for caffeine to be essentially fully cleared. This is health information, not medical advice; see a doctor if caffeine affects your heart or sleep.

en.q: How long before bed should I stop drinking caffeine?
en.a: Cut off caffeine at least 6 hours before bedtime. A peer-reviewed study found that caffeine taken 0, 3, or 6 hours before bed significantly disrupted sleep, and because the half-life is about 5 hours, even a 2 p.m. cup can still affect a slow metabolizer at 11 p.m. If you have persistent insomnia, talk with a healthcare provider.

en.q: What factors make caffeine last longer in the body?
en.a: Caffeine lasts longest in pregnant women (up to about 15 hours in the third trimester), people taking oral contraceptives (which can double the half-life), those with liver disease, and newborns (up to about 100 hours in premature infants and up to about 8 hours in full-term infants). It clears fastest in smokers (up to 50% shorter half-life). The genetics of the CYP1A2 liver enzyme drives most of the individual variation. This is health information, not medical advice; if you are pregnant or managing a liver condition, talk with your doctor about caffeine.

en.q: How long do caffeine's effects (the buzz) last?
en.a: The alert, energized feeling typically lasts 4 to 6 hours. Caffeine peaks in the blood 15 minutes to 2 hours after you drink it (often around 30-60 minutes), then gradually fades - though detectable caffeine remains in the body far longer than the felt effects. This is health information, not medical advice; if you get palpitations, anxiety, or trouble sleeping from caffeine, check in with a healthcare professional.

en.q: How long does the flu last?
en.a: For most people the flu lasts a few days to about a week, with full recovery (including any lingering cough or tiredness) within one to two weeks, though a cough and fatigue can persist longer. The CDC says most people recover in a few days to less than two weeks; Johns Hopkins Medicine notes that fever and body aches often last 3 to 7 days, while cough and fatigue may last two weeks or more. This is general information, not medical advice — see a doctor if symptoms are severe, worsening, or not improving.

en.q: How long are you contagious with the flu?
en.a: You can spread the flu from about one day before symptoms appear until roughly five to seven days after you become sick, according to the CDC. You are most contagious during the first three days of illness, and Cleveland Clinic notes contagiousness peaks in the three to four days after symptoms start. Young children and people with weakened immune systems may be contagious for longer. This is general information, not medical advice.

en.q: How long does a flu fever last?
en.a: Fever and body aches often last about 3 to 7 days and tend to go away faster than other symptoms, while a cough or runny nose can linger for two weeks or more (Johns Hopkins Medicine; Cleveland Clinic). Cleveland Clinic advises contacting a healthcare provider if your fever lasts longer than three days or your symptoms don't improve after seven to ten days. This is general information, not medical advice — seek emergency care for difficulty breathing, chest pain, confusion, a fever above 103°F/40°C (adults), or any fever in an infant under 12 weeks.

en.q: When should I take antivirals for the flu?
en.a: Prescription antiviral drugs work best when started within 48 hours of symptom onset and can shorten the illness by about a day, according to the CDC. They are most important for people at higher risk of complications, those who are very sick, or those who are hospitalized, though starting later can still help in those cases. Antibiotics do not treat the flu because it is a virus. This is descriptive, not medical advice — ask a healthcare provider whether antivirals are appropriate for you, and seek emergency care for difficulty breathing, chest pain, confusion, or dehydration.

en.q: How long does a common cold last?
en.a: Most colds last 7 to 10 days in adults and older children. The Cleveland Clinic and MedlinePlus (NIH) put typical recovery at about a week to 10 days, while the Merck Manual notes that symptoms usually resolve within 10 days. The first symptoms typically appear within 1 to 3 days, symptoms often peak around days 4 to 7, and a cough can linger into the second week. This is health information, not medical advice — see a doctor if symptoms last more than 10 days, you have a high or persistent fever, or you have trouble breathing.

en.q: How long is a cold contagious?
en.a: You can be contagious for up to two weeks, including a day or two before symptoms appear, according to the Cleveland Clinic. You are most contagious when symptoms are at their worst — usually the first two to three days you feel sick (Cleveland Clinic; MedlinePlus). The Merck Manual adds that a cold is most contagious during the first 1 to 2 days after symptoms develop. This is health information, not medical advice; contact a healthcare provider with any concerning symptoms.

en.q: Do antibiotics help a cold?
en.a: No. Colds are caused by viruses, and antibiotics only treat bacterial infections, so they will not help you recover and can cause side effects — including rash, severe allergic reactions, antimicrobial-resistant infections, and C. diff infection (CDC). The CDC, Cleveland Clinic, and Merck Manual stress that even thick or colored mucus does not mean you need antibiotics. They are only useful if a bacterial complication, such as an ear infection or pneumonia, develops. This is health information, not medical advice; see a doctor if your symptoms worsen or do not improve.

en.q: When should I see a doctor for a cold?
en.a: See a doctor if symptoms last more than 10 days without improving, if you have a high fever or a fever lasting longer than four days (CDC), or if a fever returns after clearing. Seek emergency or urgent care for trouble breathing, dehydration, or symptoms that improve and then return or worsen. For babies, the American Academy of Pediatrics says call your pediatrician immediately for any fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher in an infant younger than 3 months (12 weeks); for older children, contact a provider for a fever lasting more than 24 hours (under age 2) or more than 3 days (age 2 and up). This is health information, not medical advice — in an emergency, seek care immediately.

en.q: How long does strep throat last without antibiotics?
en.a: Untreated strep throat symptoms typically ease within about a week (roughly 5 to 7 days), though the full course can sometimes run toward 7 to 10 days (StatPearls; Nemours KidsHealth; NHS). Without antibiotics, though, you can stay contagious for up to 2 to 3 weeks and you remain at risk of complications such as rheumatic fever or kidney inflammation, which is why clinicians still recommend seeing a doctor for treatment rather than waiting it out. This is health information, not medical advice; contact a clinician for diagnosis and care.

en.q: How long does strep throat last with antibiotics?
en.a: With an appropriate antibiotic, most people feel better within 1 to 2 days and are no longer contagious after about 24 hours of treatment (Cleveland Clinic; Nemours KidsHealth; StatPearls). A standard course lasts 10 days. Even if symptoms disappear quickly, finish the entire course to help prevent complications such as rheumatic fever (American Academy of Pediatrics). This is health information, not medical advice; a clinician should confirm the diagnosis with a throat swab before any antibiotic is prescribed.

en.q: When is strep throat no longer contagious?
en.a: After starting antibiotics, you are generally no longer contagious after 24 hours, as long as your symptoms are improving and your fever is gone (StatPearls; NHS; Cleveland Clinic). Without antibiotics, you can spread strep for up to 2 to 3 weeks (Nemours KidsHealth). The incubation period is 2 to 5 days (CDC), and you can infect others before you feel sick. This is health information, not medical advice; see a doctor if you suspect strep or if symptoms worsen.

en.q: How is strep throat diagnosed?
en.a: A clinician swabs the back of the throat and runs either a rapid strep test (results in about 5 to 20 minutes) or a throat culture (results in 1 to 2 days) (Cleveland Clinic; StatPearls; AAP). Because most sore throats are viral (CDC), the swab, not the symptoms alone, determines whether bacteria are present and whether antibiotics will help. This is health information, not medical advice; see a healthcare provider for testing rather than self-diagnosing.

en.q: How long does a viral sinus infection last?
en.a: A viral sinus infection typically lasts 7 to 10 days and usually follows a cold, clearing on its own without antibiotics. The CDC notes that most sinus infections get better on their own, and Johns Hopkins notes that viral sinus inflammation may resolve in about 10 days. This is general health information, not medical advice; see a doctor if symptoms last beyond 10 days, worsen after improving, or become severe.

en.q: How do I know if my sinus infection is bacterial?
en.a: The CDC points to several clues: symptoms lasting more than 10 days without improvement, symptoms that get worse after they seemed to be getting better (often called "double sickening"), and persistent facial pain or fever. Only a healthcare provider can confirm a bacterial infection and decide whether antibiotics are appropriate. Seek emergency care for vision changes, swelling or redness around the eyes, high fever (over 103 F/40 C), stiff neck, confusion, or seizures.

en.q: When is a sinus infection considered chronic?
en.a: Sinusitis is classified as chronic when symptoms last 12 weeks or longer despite medical treatment, according to the Cleveland Clinic and MedlinePlus (NIH). Cases lasting between 4 and 12 weeks are termed subacute, bridging acute and chronic. This is general health information, not medical advice; see a doctor for persistent or recurring symptoms.

en.q: Is a sinus infection contagious?
en.a: The sinus infection itself is not contagious, but the viruses (and bacteria) that cause it are. The Cleveland Clinic states that sinusitis is not contagious even though the germs that trigger it can be, and the CDC confirms that viruses cause most sinus infections, spreading through coughs, sneezes, and unwashed hands. This is general health information, not medical advice; see a doctor for severe or worsening symptoms.

en.q: How long does acute bronchitis typically last?
en.a: Acute bronchitis (a chest cold) usually lasts 1 to 3 weeks. The CDC defines it as symptoms lasting less than 3 weeks, and the American Lung Association notes it usually lasts a week to 10 days. The cough can linger for several weeks, and the Cleveland Clinic notes full recovery may take 3 to 6 weeks in some people. This is health information, not medical advice.

en.q: How long is bronchitis contagious?
en.a: The inflammation itself is not contagious — only the underlying virus is. Because about 90–95% of cases are viral, you can spread it through coughs and sneezes for roughly a few days to about a week after symptoms start, per the Cleveland Clinic. If the cause is bacterial (such as pertussis), you are usually no longer contagious 24 hours after starting antibiotics.

en.q: Do antibiotics help bronchitis go away faster?
en.a: Rarely. Acute bronchitis is viral in roughly 90–95% of cases, and antibiotics do not kill viruses. The CDC says antibiotics will not help and are not recommended even for most bacterial chest colds. A Cochrane review of randomized trials found antibiotics shorten the cough by only about half a day while adding side-effect risk. Antibiotics are reserved for diagnosed whooping cough or pneumonia. This is general information, not medical advice — talk to a clinician about your own case.

en.q: When should I see a doctor for bronchitis?
en.a: See a clinician if your cough lasts more than 3 weeks, you have a fever greater than 102°F (38.9°C), a fever lasting more than 5 days or reaching 104°F, you cough up blood, or you have new or worsening shortness of breath, wheezing, confusion, or bluish, pale, or blotchy lips or skin. For infants under 3 months with a fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher, contact a provider right away (CDC). Severe breathing trouble, chest pain, or confusion is an emergency — call your local emergency number. This is health information, not a substitute for medical advice.

en.q: How long does a stomach bug last in adults?
en.a: Most adults recover in 1 to 3 days — the CDC says most people with norovirus illness get better within 1 to 3 days. If rotavirus is the cause, vomiting and watery diarrhea can last 3 to 8 days. In occasional cases symptoms linger for up to 14 days.

en.q: How long are you contagious with a stomach bug?
en.a: You are most contagious while you have symptoms, and you stay contagious for up to 48 hours after they stop, according to Cleveland Clinic. The CDC warns you can still spread norovirus for 2 weeks or more after you feel better. The practical rule: stay isolated until two days after your symptoms stop, and keep washing your hands with soap and water.

en.q: How fast do stomach bug symptoms appear after exposure?
en.a: Norovirus symptoms usually develop 12 to 48 hours after exposure, per the CDC. Johns Hopkins Medicine says viral gastroenteritis symptoms often begin about 1 to 2 days after the virus enters the body, and Mayo Clinic puts the window at 1 to 3 days depending on the cause. Because the virus can be present in your stool before symptoms start, you may spread it before you feel sick.

en.q: When should you go to the doctor for a stomach bug?
en.a: Adults should call a provider if they cannot keep liquids down for 24 hours, have vomited or had diarrhea for more than two days, run a fever above 104 F (40 C), vomit blood, notice blood in bowel movements or severe stomach pain, or show dehydration signs like dry mouth, deep yellow urine, or dizziness. Cleveland Clinic adds: no improvement after four days, or a fever above 102 F lasting four days. For children and infants the bar is lower — call right away for a fever of 102 F (38.9 C) or higher, bloody diarrhea, no wet diaper in six hours, or unusual sleepiness.

en.q: How long does pink eye usually last?
en.a: Most pink eye clears within 1 to 2 weeks. Viral pink eye, the most common kind, usually lasts 7 to 14 days, though most mild cases resolve within 5 to 7 days and some linger 2 to 3 weeks or more. Bacterial pink eye often clears in 2 to 5 days, and allergic pink eye continues as long as you are exposed to the trigger.

en.q: How long is pink eye contagious?
en.a: Viral and bacterial pink eye are very contagious, while allergic and irritant pink eye are not contagious at all. You can spread it before symptoms even appear, so the safest rule is to treat it as contagious while the eyes are still red with discharge. Antibiotics help stop bacterial pink eye from spreading, which is why many schools allow children back 24 hours after drops begin.

en.q: When can my child go back to school with pink eye?
en.a: For bacterial pink eye, many schools allow return 24 hours after antibiotic drops begin, once the discharge has dwindled to a small amount. For viral pink eye there is no drops shortcut — the AAO advises staying home until the eyes are no longer red with discharge, though the AAP notes that mild cold-related pinkeye may not require missing any school. Keep any child home who has a fever or feels generally ill.

en.q: How can I tell if pink eye is viral or bacterial?
en.a: Viral pink eye usually causes burning, red eyes with a watery discharge and often arrives alongside a cold, while bacterial pink eye tends to produce thicker yellow-green pus that can stick the eyelashes together. Allergic conjunctivitis brings intense itching and usually affects both eyes. A clinician confirms the cause from your symptoms and an eye exam — and antibiotics only help the bacterial kind.

en.q: How long does shingles last?
en.a: Most shingles rashes scab over in 7 to 10 days and clear up within 2 to 4 weeks, and the full illness usually runs about 3 to 5 weeks from the first symptoms until the skin is completely clear. Starting antiviral medicine within 72 hours of your first symptoms can shorten the course. In some cases, mostly in older adults, nerve pain called postherpetic neuralgia continues for months or years after the rash heals.

en.q: How long are you contagious with shingles?
en.a: You are contagious from the time the blisters appear until they have dried and scabbed over, which the CDC says typically takes 7 to 10 days. The virus spreads through direct contact with fluid from the blisters, and someone who catches it develops chickenpox, not shingles. Keep the rash covered and avoid contact with people who have never had chickenpox or the vaccine, pregnant women, newborns, and anyone with a weakened immune system.

en.q: How long does shingles pain last after the rash heals?
en.a: For most people the pain fades as the skin heals, but the CDC reports that about 10% to 18% of shingles patients develop postherpetic neuralgia — nerve pain in the rash area that lasts for months or even years.
